strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: multimodal severe weather warning generation from high-dimensional meteorological fields. A benchmark connecting ERA5 fields with warning text at this scale could be useful to both vision-language and geoscience communities.
MP-Bench is potentially valuable in scope, with 421,363 entries over 2023-2024, seven severe weather categories plus normal weather, multiple QA formulations, and nationwide coverage across China.

The model design is motivated by real structure in meteorological data. The temporal gating, spatial Gaussian masking from queried coordinates, and channel/pressure-level attention are simple but relevant mechanisms for time, geography, and vertical atmospheric structure.

The experiments include several contemporary MLLM backbones and an ablation of the three proposed modules. The ablation suggests that the modules are complementary, especially for T/F and regional severe-weather classification.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim is not technically well supported. The input is described as ERA5 reanalysis from the 12 hours starting at the warning issuance time, i.e. data from or after the target warning period. This is not operationally available at warning time and makes the task closer to retrospective diagnosis or warning-text reconstruction than severe weather prediction. The paper repeatedly frames the system as an end-to-end AI weather station, but the experimental setup does not establish real forecasting skill from past observations or NWP forecasts.

The evaluation is insufficient to justify the broad claims. There is no comparison to strong non-MLLM baselines such as supervised classifiers/regressors on ERA5, weather-specific deep models, retrieval/template systems, or operational warning heuristics. The GPT-4o baseline is particularly weak and arguably unfair because high-dimensional meteorology is compressed into a three-channel image, so its poor score does not strongly validate the proposed method.

The main Table 2 compares only open-source models after adding all proposed modules, so it does not isolate the contribution of MMLM versus backbone fine-tuning. The ablation uses a separate 5,000-instance sample and reports much lower full-model performance than the main table, making the relationship between the ablation and the headline results unclear.

Dataset construction and reproducibility details are incomplete. The paper does not fully specify grid extents/resolution after cropping, exact tensor shapes, QA generation procedure, split sizes, negative-sampling protocol, duplicate/event overlap handling, or whether CMA warning text can be redistributed. There are also inconsistencies in variable descriptions: the main text mentions temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, and pressure, while the appendix lists z, u, v, t, q.

The task labels are derived from issued warnings, not independently verified severe-weather observations. This means the model may learn CMA warning policy, station-specific patterns, or template/seasonal priors rather than physical event occurrence. The paper does not evaluate spatial generalization to held-out regions, future-year robustness beyond a subset of 2024, or performance under rare but high-impact categories.

Metrics are shallow for the claimed application. MC/T/F/RSW accuracies obscure class imbalance and false alarm/miss tradeoffs, which are critical for warnings. NSW relies on GPT-4o scoring without reported human validation or scorer reliability. Snowstorm accuracy is reported as below 6%, which is a serious limitation for a severe-weather warning benchmark despite being attributed to imbalance.

The presentation contains several clarity and correctness issues that reduce confidence: repeated/incorrect QA type names, “four options” for MC despite many listed choices, inconsistent module naming, formula notation problems, and claims such as “36.01% overall gain” that appear to report an absolute score rather than a gain. These are not merely stylistic because they affect interpretation of the method and results.

strengths: The application target is important: automating severe-weather warning interpretation from meteorological fields is socially useful and technically relevant to multimodal learning beyond natural images.

MP-Bench appears sizable, with 421,363 ERA5-warning pairs covering multiple severe-weather categories across China, and the paper makes a useful attempt to define several QA-style tasks rather than only single-label classification.

The model components are simple and plausible for the domain: temporal differencing/gating, coordinate-centered spatial masking, and pressure-level/channel attention are reasonable inductive biases for gridded meteorological data.
The ablation table suggests that the three modules improve over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline on the sampled evaluation subset, especially for T/F and RSW tasks.
weaknesses: The core task formulation does not convincingly support the paper's claim of severe weather prediction or an operational AI warning system. The input uses ERA5 reanalysis data from [t, t+11] starting at the warning issuance time, i.e. future analyzed atmospheric states relative to issuance, rather than forecast data available before warning release. This risks turning the task into post-hoc warning reconstruction rather than prediction.

Ground truth is CMA warning text, not verified observed severe-weather occurrence. Since warnings are human/system products that may be based on NWP and expert judgment, the model may be learning to imitate warning issuance patterns rather than learning meteorological event occurrence or warning skill. The paper does not discuss false alarms, missed events, lead time, or standard meteorological verification metrics.

The experimental comparison is weak and somewhat misleading. The main table compares GPT-4o to open-source models that are all enhanced with the proposed modules, so it does not isolate the contribution of MMLM. The closed-source GPT-4o baseline is handicapped by an ad hoc conversion of meteorological fields to three-channel inputs, making the comparison uninformative.

Absolute performance remains poor on important parts of the benchmark. MC-sub is only 58.19 for the best model, NSW is 2.1/5, and snowstorm accuracy is reported below 6%, despite the paper's strong claims that the model performs exceptionally well across multiple tasks.

Evaluation breadth is limited. There is no comparison to standard meteorological or spatiotemporal baselines, no evaluation on held-out regions or years beyond a subset of 2024, no uncertainty or calibration analysis, and no operational lead-time study. These omissions are material for a forecasting paper.

Several methodological details are unclear or inconsistent. The paper alternates between variables such as precipitation/pressure and the appendix's z/u/v/t/q list; MC is described as four options although the appendix shows many severity-coded options; RSW is duplicated in the introduction; and some equations/notational definitions are imprecise.

The proposed architecture is not very original from a computer vision/multimodal modeling perspective. The modules are relatively standard gating, Gaussian masking, and channel-attention mechanisms adapted to ERA5, and the paper does not provide enough evidence that these are the right or necessary design choices beyond a small ablation subset.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper states that code and data will be released, but the manuscript itself lacks sufficient details on data cleaning, warning-to-grid matching, exact train/test split, coordinate extraction, spatial extent/cropping, negative sampling, and GPT-based scoring reliability to independently reproduce the results.

Presentation quality raises confidence concerns: there are multiple grammar issues, duplicated/mislabeled tables, unclear metric descriptions, and overclaimed conclusions. These are not merely cosmetic because they obscure the exact experimental setup and interpretation of the reported numbers.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: turning high-dimensional meteorological fields into actionable severe-weather warnings. The proposed MP-Bench dataset is a strong contribution, with 421,363 aligned ERA5-warning pairs across China, seven severe-weather types plus normal samples, multiple QA formats, and a temporal split using 2023 for training and 2024 for testing.

The work makes a credible case that raw 4D meteorological inputs are useful compared with compressing fields into image-like representations. The three modules target meaningful structure in the data: temporal changes, location-conditioned spatial focus, and pressure-level/channel selection.

The empirical results are encouraging. Qwen2.5-VL with the proposed modules substantially outperforms the GPT-4o image-based setup and other adapted open-source MLLMs across MC, T/F, RSW, and NSW tasks. The ablation study also shows consistent gains when all three modules are combined, especially for T/F and RSW.

The appendix adds useful dataset statistics, prompt examples, training hyperparameters, and qualitative/interpretability-style analyses of temporal and pressure-level weights. These details make the benchmark and model easier to understand than many comparable dataset papers.

The paper is potentially useful to both computer vision/multimodal learning and applied meteorology communities, especially as a benchmark for structured reasoning over non-natural-image spatiotemporal scientific data.
weaknesses: A central limitation is that the dataset uses ERA5 reanalysis fields from the 12 hours after warning issuance. This weakens the claim of operational severe-weather prediction: unless these inputs are meant to approximate unavailable future NWP forecasts, the task is closer to retrospective warning reconstruction from future reanalysis than real-time forecasting. The paper should be much clearer about this distinction.

The labels are warning records rather than verified observed severe-weather events. CMA warnings reflect operational decisions and may include false alarms, missed events, policy thresholds, and regional reporting biases. Thus the model may learn to imitate warning issuance patterns rather than physical event occurrence.

The experimental comparison is somewhat hard to interpret because Table 2 reports open-source models after adding all proposed modules, rather than clean baseline models versus baseline-plus-modules on the full evaluation set. The only ablation is on a 5,000-sample subset, so the magnitude of the module contribution on the main benchmark remains uncertain.

The GPT-4o baseline is not a strong or fully fair reference point: the authors convert only a few surface variables into a three-channel representation, while their method consumes richer 4D fields. The very low GPT-4o scores therefore establish that this particular encoding is poor, but not necessarily that closed-source MLLMs are intrinsically unsuitable.

Evaluation of the NSW task relies on GPT-4o scoring without reported human validation, inter-rater checks, or robustness analysis. Since NSW is the most open-ended and operationally relevant task, this limits confidence in the reported 0-5 scores.

Some methodological details are underspecified or internally inconsistent. The main text says selected variables include temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, and pressure, while the appendix lists z, u, v, t, and q. The MC metric description says four options, but the appendix prompt contains many severity-category options. The subset of 2024 used for testing is not fully specified.

The QA templates and inclusion of coordinates may allow models to exploit regional climatology, warning priors, and templated answer formats. More analysis is needed to separate meteorological-field reasoning from location/type prior learning, especially given the strong class imbalance such as very few snowstorm examples.

The proposed modules are sensible but technically simple, and the paper sometimes overstates novelty relative to existing attention, gating, and spatial masking mechanisms. The main novelty is stronger as a dataset/task formulation than as a modeling contribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: code and dataset are promised but not available in the paper, preprocessing details are limited, and exact train/test sample counts per QA type are not fully reported. This is likely fixable, but it matters for a benchmark paper.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored multimodal problem: converting high-dimensional meteorological fields into actionable severe-weather warning text. The proposed MP-Bench dataset is potentially valuable due to its scale, year-wise split, multiple QA formats, and coverage of seven severe-weather categories plus normal cases.

The method is designed around meteorological structure rather than treating the data purely as images. The temporal gating, spatial coordinate masking, and pressure-level/channel attention modules are plausible inductive biases for ERA5-like 4D fields.

The experiments compare several strong open-source MLLM backbones and show consistent gains for the proposed MMLM variants over 3-channel fine-tuned baselines. The best Qwen2.5-VL-based model improves MC-main accuracy from 56.26 to 72.37 and T/F accuracy from 68.33 to 87.13 in Table 2.

The paper includes useful ablations and supplemental analyses, including module ablations, temporal-window comparisons, cross-year testing, a small US generalization study, and visualizations intended to connect learned weights with meteorological interpretation.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim is not technically supported because the model input is ERA5 reanalysis from the 12 hours starting at the warning issuance time, i.e. [t,t+11]. ERA5 is retrospective analysis, and much of this window is future information relative to issuance. This makes the task closer to post-hoc warning reconstruction from future atmospheric fields, not operational early warning or severe-weather prediction as claimed.

The labels are warning records rather than verified severe-weather occurrences. The paper does not sufficiently discuss how human warning policy, station practices, false alarms, missed events, and regional population/station density biases affect the target. The added normal samples are sampled across regions/seasons, but the manuscript does not establish that they are true non-event cases under the same verification standard.

The evaluation does not cleanly isolate the contribution of the proposed modules. The main baseline uses only 3-channel/3-level meteorological input, while MMLM uses 185 channels plus new modules, so improvements conflate richer input with architectural changes. The module ablation is only on a 5,000-sample subset and does not match the main Table 2 results, limiting the strength of the causal claims.

Some technical details are internally inconsistent or underspecified. The text says the selected variables include precipitation and pressure, but the appendix table lists z, u, v, t, and q over 37 pressure levels, with no precipitation variable. The TGCA equations have unclear tensor shapes and attention normalization, and important implementation choices such as grid extent, masking width sigma, coordinate extraction, and tokenization/projection details are not fully specified.

The reported absolute performance remains limited for the more informative tasks. The best MC-sub Macro-F1 is only 29.31, indicating weak performance on fine-grained/severity or rare categories, and the best NSW score is 2.1/5 under an LLM-judge rubric. These results are useful but do not justify the paper's stronger language about accurate automated warning generation.

The NSW evaluation relies on GPT-4o as a judge without human validation, judge agreement analysis, or robustness checks. This is particularly concerning because the task involves structured meteorological warnings where location, category, and severity errors have different operational implications.

The closed-source GPT-4o comparison is not very informative or fair: the input is converted into a limited visual/three-channel representation, and the near-zero T/F accuracy suggests a possible prompt/input mismatch rather than a meaningful estimate of closed-source model capability.

The cross-geographical generalization experiment is too thin to support broad generalization claims. It uses only 1,000 NOAA samples, only MC-main categories, unclear category mapping and temporal alignment, and no detailed per-category or baseline table in the main text.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time. The code and dataset are only promised, training/evaluation tables contain placeholder paths, and several dataset-construction choices needed to reproduce MP-Bench are missing or ambiguous.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant problem: connecting high-dimensional meteorological fields with severe-weather warning text, which is a meaningful direction for computer vision/multimodal learning beyond standard image-language benchmarks.

MP-Bench could be a useful resource if released with adequate documentation. Its scale is substantial, with 421,363 warning/normal samples over 2023-2024, multiple severe-weather categories, regional/national QA formats, and a temporal split.

The proposed modules are motivated by reasonable meteorological structure: temporal changes, spatial localization from coordinates, and vertical pressure-level/channel selection. The ablations suggest these components improve over the authors' own 3-channel MLLM baselines.

The manuscript includes some supplementary analysis of pressure-level attention and temporal weighting patterns, which is a useful attempt to connect learned behavior to physical meteorological interpretation.
weaknesses: The central task formulation is not convincingly a forecasting setup. The model ingests ERA5 reanalysis fields from the 12 hours after warning issuance, i.e. [t,t+11], which uses analyzed meteorological states that would not be available at warning time in an operational early-warning system. This makes the claimed 'prediction' and 'AI weather station' framing substantially overstated; the task is closer to post-hoc warning classification/description from reanalysis data.

The evaluation lacks strong and appropriate meteorological baselines. There is no comparison to threshold/rule-based warning criteria, classical ML, CNN/Transformer classifiers over ERA5 grids, or modern weather foundation models adapted to warning labels. The closed-source GPT-4o baseline is especially weakly constructed and not informative, since high-dimensional meteorology is compressed into a three-channel visual input that GPT-4o was not designed to interpret.

The reported performance is not strong enough to support the broad claims. The best MC-sub Macro-F1 is only 29.31, NSW reaches only 2.1/5, and several baselines have very low Macro-F1 despite moderate accuracy, indicating serious rare-class and severity-level weaknesses. These are critical for severe-weather warning applications, where rare high-impact events matter most.

The ablation design confounds architecture and input information. The main baseline uses only 3 pressure-level/channel inputs, while MMLM uses 185 pressure-level channels plus the proposed modules. This does not isolate whether gains come from the modules, the additional meteorological variables/levels, or model capacity. The 5,000-sample ablation subset also reports substantially different numbers from the full experiment, making conclusions harder to interpret.

Dataset labels and negative samples raise concerns. CMA warnings reflect human-issued alerts rather than verified event occurrence, and 'normal weather' samples are sampled from absence of warnings, which may include missed events or benign but meteorologically extreme cases. The paper does not sufficiently discuss label noise, warning policy changes, regional reporting bias, or station/administrative duplication.

The cross-geographical generalization experiment is under-specified and weak. The NOAA subset contains only 1,000 samples, only category labels, and unclear alignment to ERA5-like inputs and Chinese warning categories. A 64.20 accuracy / 35.18 Macro-F1 result is not enough to establish robust geographic generalization.

Technical details are often vague or inconsistent. The manuscript alternates between variables such as temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, and pressure, while the supplementary table lists z, u, v, t, q and omits precipitation. Spatial grid size, exact cropping, preprocessing, coordinate parsing, sigma choice for TGS, tokenization/projection details, and fusion implementation are not described at a reproducible level.

Some mathematical descriptions appear dimensionally unclear, especially TGCA's attention equation, and the role of the LLM relative to the meteorological encoder is underspecified. It is difficult to determine whether the model is learning genuine multimodal reasoning or mostly supervised classification with text-formatted prompts.

The NSW metric relies on GPT-4o-as-judge, but the rubric is coarse, exact-location matching is not clearly operationalized, and no validation against human expert scoring is reported. This weakens confidence in the open-ended generation results.

The paper's claims are more ambitious than the evidence supports. The contribution may be valuable as a dataset and exploratory architecture, but the current experimental protocol, baseline selection, reproducibility gaps, and leakage-like use of future reanalysis data make the acceptance case weak.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: connecting high-dimensional meteorological fields with operational severe-weather warning text. The proposed MP-Bench dataset is a substantial contribution, with 421k paired samples, multiple severe weather types, a year-wise train/test split, and several QA formats spanning classification and generation.

The model design is well motivated for the domain. DTGF, TGS, and TGCA target temporal evolution, geographic focus, and vertical/channel selection respectively, which are sensible inductive biases for 4D meteorological data.

The empirical results support the main direction. Across four MLLM backbones, adding the proposed MMLM components improves performance over the corresponding baselines, with the strongest Qwen2.5-VL variant reaching 72.37 MC-main accuracy, 50.88 MC-main Macro-F1, 87.13 T/F accuracy, and 71.23 RSW accuracy.
The paper includes useful ablations of the three modules and temporal window length, plus some interpretability analysis showing attention over physically meaningful time windows and pressure levels.
The manuscript is generally clear about dataset construction, task definitions, and training setup, and the supplementary material provides useful statistics and examples.
weaknesses: The evaluation has an important ambiguity: the inputs are ERA5 reanalysis fields over [t, t+11] after warning issuance. If the intended system is real-time forecasting, it is unclear whether these future fields correspond to information actually available at issuance time, or whether this setup uses post hoc reanalysis that could make the task easier than operational forecasting.

The labels are warnings issued by meteorological agencies rather than independently verified severe-weather outcomes. This means the model may learn warning issuance patterns, institutional thresholds, or false-alarm behavior, not necessarily physical event occurrence. The paper should separate warning prediction from event prediction more carefully.

The main baseline comparison conflates architecture and input information. Baselines use only 3-channel meteorological inputs, while MMLM uses 185 pressure-level channels plus new fusion modules, so the gains cannot be attributed cleanly to the proposed modules alone.

Some reported absolute performance remains modest for the harder and more operationally relevant tasks: MC-sub Macro-F1 is 29.31 for the best model and NSW score is only 2.1/5. This suggests severity-level recognition and national-scale generation are still far from reliable.

The ablation study is conducted on only a 5,000-sample subset and gives much lower full-module performance than the main table, making it hard to judge whether module contributions scale to the full dataset. Some individual module combinations also degrade particular metrics, but the discussion mostly emphasizes improvements.

The NSW evaluation relies on GPT-4o as an automatic judge. Although a rubric is provided, there is no reported validation against human meteorological assessment, inter-rater agreement, or sensitivity analysis of the judge, which weakens confidence in the open-ended results.

Cross-geographic generalization is promising but limited: the NOAA evaluation uses only 1,000 samples and only MC-main category prediction, without severity, regional text generation, or detailed mapping between CMA and NOAA event definitions.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time. The paper says code and dataset will be released, but current training/evaluation tables contain placeholder paths, and details such as preprocessing, coordinate extraction, negative sampling, and exact class mappings are not sufficient for full independent replication.
